name: Trader test battery, version 2
models: Reported, as of Nov 2026: the Optiver, IMC and Citadel Securities test batteries. Number sequences, probability at speed, and likelihood ranking with intervals.
description: These are reported formats from the Optiver, IMC and Citadel Securities test batteries, as described by Nov 2026. There are three papers, each on its own clock. Sequences is 15 questions in 25 minutes, one at a time, with no skipping. Probability at speed is 15 questions in 30 minutes; you may move between them. Likelihood ranking and intervals is 10 questions in 10 minutes. Wrong answers score 0, and no calculator is allowed. Firms mix and rename these papers, so expect a different order on the day. This is version 2 of 3.

items.title: Equal gaps
items.question: What comes next? 13, 19, 25, 31, 37, ?

options.why: You were one out. Check the last step again.
You doubled the last term. The gaps are equal, not the ratios.
You added the gap of 6 twice.

feedback.correct: The gap is +6 each time.
feedback.generic: Find the gap between neighbours, with its sign.

explain.text: Each term is 6 more than the one before. So the next is $37 + 6 = 43$.

options.why: You were one out. Multiply the last term again.
You added the last gap of 112 again. The gaps grow too.
You multiplied by 3. Each term is 2 times the one before.

feedback.correct: Each term is 2 times the one before.
feedback.generic: Divide each term by the one before it.

explain.text: The ratio is 2 throughout. So the next is $2 \times 224 = 448$.

items.title: Squares shifted
items.question: What comes next? 6, 13, 22, 33, 46, ?

options.why: You added the last gap of 13 again. The gaps grow by 2.
You gave $8^2$ and dropped the −3.
You doubled the last term. The gaps grow by 2, so look for squares.

feedback.correct: Each term is a square minus 3: $8^2 - 3 = 61$.
feedback.generic: Compare each term with the nearest square.

explain.text: The terms are $n^2 - 3$ for $n = 3$ to $7$. The next is $8^2 - 3 = 61$. Check: the gaps rise by 2, so the next gap is 15.

items.title: Double and adjust
items.question: What comes next? 1, 5, 13, 29, 61, ?

options.why: You doubled and then took away 3: the sign is wrong.
You repeated the last gap of 32. The gaps double.
You doubled 61 and left out the +3.

feedback.correct: Double, then add 3.
feedback.generic: Try doubling each term and see what is left over.

explain.text: Each term is double the one before, plus 3. So the next is $2 \times 61 + 3 = 125$. Check: the gaps double, so the next gap is 64.

options.why: You were two short. Each gap is 1 more than the last.
You repeated the last gap of 8. The gaps grow by 1.
You doubled the last term. Look at the gaps instead.

feedback.correct: The gaps grow by 1: the next gap is 9.
feedback.generic: Write down the gaps, then the gaps between the gaps.

explain.text: The gaps are 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, rising by 1 each time. So the next gap is 9 and the next term is $40 + 9 = 49$.

items.title: Two steps in turn
items.question: What comes next? 3, 9, 5, 15, 11, 33, ?

options.why: You took away 3, not 4.
You repeated the last gap of 22.
You multiplied by 3 again. The steps take turns: $\times 3$, then $-4$.

feedback.correct: The steps take turns, $\times 3$ then $-4$. Next is $- 4$.
feedback.generic: Look at the steps one at a time: they are not all the same kind.

explain.text: The steps go $\times 3$, $-4$, $\times 3$, $-4$ in turn. The next step is $- 4$, so $33 - 4 = 29$.

items.title: Sum of the two before
items.question: What comes next? 1, 5, 6, 11, 17, 28, ?

options.why: You were one out. Add the last two terms again.
You doubled the last term. Add the two before instead.
You repeated the last gap of 11.

feedback.correct: Each term is the sum of the two before: $17 + 28 = 45$.
feedback.generic: Add two neighbours and compare with the term after them.

explain.text: Each term is the sum of the two before it. So the next is $17 + 28 = 45$. Check: the gaps are the earlier terms, so the next gap is 17.

options.why: You applied the odd-place rule, +5. The eighth term is an even place.
You added the last two terms. The two lists take turns.
You added 3 to 34, not 2.

feedback.correct: Two lists take turns. The even places go +2, so $34 + 2 = 36$.
feedback.generic: Read every other term on its own.

explain.text: The odd places go 2, 7, 12, 17, and the even places go 30, 32, 34. The eighth term is an even place, so it is $34 + 2 = 36$.

options.why: You were two out. Add the digits of the last term again.
You doubled the last term.
You repeated the last gap of 8.

feedback.correct: Add the digit sum: $70 + 7 = 77$.
feedback.generic: Compare each gap with the digits of the term before it.

explain.text: Each gap is the digit sum of the term before: $23 + 5 = 28$, and so on. The last term 70 has digit sum 7, so the next is 77.

options.why: You doubled the last term. These are the primes in order.
You repeated the last gap of 2, but 45 is not prime.
You were one out. The next prime is odd.

feedback.correct: These are the primes in order. The next prime after 43 is 47.
feedback.generic: Each term is a number with a special property. Which numbers are missing?

explain.text: Every term is prime and none is skipped. After 43, the numbers 44, 45, 46 are not prime, so the next is 47.

items.title: Cubes shifted
items.question: What comes next? 4, 11, 30, 67, 128, ?

options.why: You gave $6^3$ and dropped the +3.
You repeated the last gap of 61. The gaps grow faster each time.
You doubled the last term. Compare the terms with the cubes.

feedback.correct: Each term is a cube plus 3: $6^3 + 3 = 219$.
feedback.generic: Compare each term with 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, ...

explain.text: The terms are $n^3 + 3$ for $n = 1$ to $5$. So the next is $6^3 + 3 = 216 + 3 = 219$.

items.title: Two ratios in turn
items.question: What comes next? 5, 1, 10, 3, 20, 9, 40, ?

options.why: You applied the odd-place rule, $\times 2$. The eighth term is an even place.
You doubled 9. The even places go $\times 3$.
You added the last two terms.

feedback.correct: The even places go $\times 3$, so $9 \times 3 = 27$.
feedback.generic: Read the odd places and the even places as two lists.

explain.text: The odd places go 5, 10, 20, 40 ($\times 2$). The even places go 1, 3, 9 ($\times 3$). The eighth term is an even place: $9 \times 3 = 27$.

options.why: You repeated the last gap of 24. The gaps grow by 2.
You doubled the last term.
You squared 14. Each term is two neighbours multiplied.

feedback.correct: Each term is $n(n + 1)$: $13 \times 14 = 182$.
feedback.generic: Write each term as a product of two whole numbers close together.

explain.text: The terms are $8 \times 9$, $9 \times 10$, and so on. So the next is $13 \times 14 = 182$. Check: the gaps rise by 2, so the next gap is 26.

items.title: A rising multiplier
items.question: What comes next? 2, 3, 7, 22, 89, ?

options.why: You multiplied by 5 and left out the + 1.
You raised the multiplier by 2, to 6.
You repeated the last gap of 67.

feedback.correct: Multiply by a number that rises by 1 each step, then add 1: $5 \times 89 + 1 = 446$.
feedback.generic: Divide each term by the one before. What do the ratios do?

explain.text: The chain is $1 \times 2 + 1 = 3$, $2 \times 3 + 1 = 7$, $3 \times 7 + 1 = 22$, $4 \times 22 + 1 = 89$. The multiplier rises by 1 each step, so the next is $5 \times 89 + 1 = 446$.

items.title: Sum of the three before
items.question: What comes next? 2, 3, 4, 9, 16, 29, 54, ?

options.why: You added only the last two terms. Each term is the sum of three.
You doubled the last term.
You repeated the last gap of 25.

feedback.correct: Each term is the sum of the three before: $16 + 29 + 54 = 99$.
feedback.generic: Try adding two terms, then three, and compare with the next.

explain.text: From the fourth term on, each is the sum of the three before it. So the next is $16 + 29 + 54 = 99$. Check: $54 \times 2 - 9 = 99$ gives the same.

items.title: A total of 10
items.question: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the chance that the total is 10?

options.why: You found the chance that the total is not 10.
You treated the 11 totals as equally likely. A middle total has more ways.
You counted each pair twice. There are 3 ordered pairs, not 6.

feedback.correct: 3 of the 36 ordered pairs make 10.
feedback.generic: List the ordered pairs that make the total, out of 36.

explain.text: The pairs (4, 6), (5, 5), (6, 4) make 10. That is 3 of 36, so $\tfrac{1}{12}$.

items.title: Exactly 2 heads in 6
items.question: A fair coin is tossed 6 times. What is the chance of exactly 2 heads?

options.why: You took 2 heads out of 6 tosses as the chance.
You found the chance of anything but exactly 2 heads.
You counted one order only. There are $\binom{6}{2} = 15$ orders.

feedback.correct: $\binom{6}{2} = 15$ orders, each $\tfrac{1}{64}$.
feedback.generic: Count the orders, then multiply by the chance of one order.

explain.text: There are $\binom{6}{2} = 15$ orders, each with chance $\tfrac{1}{64}$. So the chance is $\tfrac{15}{64} = \tfrac{15}{64}$. Listing all 64 sequences finds the same 15.

items.title: At least one six in two
items.question: A fair die is rolled twice. What is the chance of at least one six?

options.why: You added $\tfrac16$ twice. That counts the double six twice.
You found the chance that both rolls are sixes.
You found the chance of no six at all.

feedback.correct: One minus the chance of no six: $1 - \tfrac{25}{36}$.
feedback.generic: Find the chance of no six first.

explain.text: No six has chance $(\tfrac56)^2 = \tfrac{25}{36}$. So at least one six is $\tfrac{11}{36}$. Listing the 36 pairs gives 11 with a six.

items.title: Ace after ace
items.question: Two cards are dealt from a full deck. The first is an ace. What is the chance that the second is an ace?

options.why: You took the card away but still counted 4 aces.
You put the first card back. With it gone, 3 of the 51 left are aces.
You found the chance that both are aces, not the second given the first.

feedback.correct: 3 aces are left among 51 cards: $\tfrac{3}{51} = \tfrac{1}{17}$.
feedback.generic: Take the first card out, then count what is left.

explain.text: After an ace, 3 of the 51 cards left are aces, so $\tfrac{3}{51} = \tfrac{1}{17}$. Check: both aces is $\tfrac{1}{221}$, and dividing by $\tfrac{1}{13}$ gives $\tfrac{1}{17}$.

items.title: One suit, small deck
items.question: A deck has 20 cards: 5 in each of 4 suits. Two cards are dealt. What is the chance they share a suit?

options.why: You named one suit and dealt with replacement.
You dealt with replacement. With one card gone, only 4 of 19 match.
You found the chance of two of one named suit.

feedback.correct: The first card sets the suit; 4 of the 19 left match it.
feedback.generic: Let the first card choose the suit, then count the matches left.

explain.text: The first card sets the suit, and 4 of the 19 cards left match it: $\tfrac{4}{19}$. Counting pairs: $4\binom52 = 40$ of $\binom{20}{2} = 190$ agree.

items.title: Two rerolls
items.question: You roll a fair die. You may reroll up to twice, keeping the last face you roll. Playing well, what is the expected face you keep?

options.why: You allowed only one reroll. With two left, a 4 is worth rerolling.
You averaged only the faces you keep, 5 and 6.
You ignored the rerolls. That is the average of one roll.

feedback.correct: With two rerolls left, keep only 5 or 6, against $\tfrac{17}{4}$.
feedback.generic: Work back from the last roll: what is one reroll worth?

explain.text: One reroll is worth $\tfrac{17}{4}$, so on the first roll keep only 5 or 6. Then $\tfrac{5 + 6}{6} + \tfrac46 \cdot \tfrac{17}{4} = \tfrac{14}{3}$. Trying every keep rule at each stage gives the same.

items.title: Four different faces
items.question: Four fair dice are rolled. What is the chance that all four faces differ?

options.why: You found the chance that two or more faces match.
You counted sets of faces, one order only. Each set has 24 orders.
You multiplied in a fourth factor, $\tfrac26$. The first die is free.

feedback.correct: $1 \cdot \tfrac56 \cdot \tfrac46 \cdot \tfrac36 = \tfrac{5}{18}$.
feedback.generic: Roll the dice one at a time. Each must avoid the faces already shown.

explain.text: The dice must avoid 0, 1, 2 and 3 faces in turn: $\tfrac56 \cdot \tfrac46 \cdot \tfrac36 = \tfrac{5}{18}$. Counting: $6 \cdot 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 = 360$ of 1296.

items.title: First hit on the third
items.question: A signal is right on a quarter of days, independently. What is the chance its first right day is the third?

options.why: You used only the third day. The first two must be wrong as well.
You found at least one right day in three.
You made every day right.

feedback.correct: Two misses then a hit: $(\tfrac34)^2 \cdot \tfrac14$.
feedback.generic: Write the days in order: what must the first two do?

explain.text: Days one and two miss and day three hits: $\tfrac34 \cdot \tfrac34 \cdot \tfrac14 = \tfrac{9}{64}$. Listing the 64 equally likely patterns gives 9 of that shape.

items.title: Two quants of three
items.question: A desk of 6 traders and 4 quants picks a team of 3 at random. What is the chance of exactly 2 quants?

options.why: You picked with replacement, as if one person could be chosen twice.
You counted one order only, quant, quant, trader. There are 3 orders.
You found the chance of anything but exactly 2 quants.

feedback.correct: $\binom42 \binom61 = 36$ teams of $\binom{10}{3} = 120$.
feedback.generic: Count the teams that fit, then divide by all teams.

explain.text: Choose 2 of 4 quants and 1 of 6 traders: $6 \cdot 6 = 36$ of $\binom{10}{3} = 120$ teams, so $\tfrac{3}{10}$. Listing all 120 teams finds the same 36.

items.title: Both red
items.question: An urn holds 4 red and 2 blue balls. You draw 2 without replacement. What is the chance both are red?

options.why: You found the chance that at least one is blue.
You drew with replacement. After a red, 3 of 5 are red.
You used only the first draw.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac46 \cdot \tfrac35 = \tfrac25$.
feedback.generic: Multiply the chances, removing the first ball.

explain.text: The first is red with chance $\tfrac46$, then the second with $\tfrac35$. So $\tfrac{12}{30} = \tfrac25$. Counting: $\binom42 = 6$ of $\binom62 = 15$ pairs.

items.title: Stocks that pass
items.question: 20% of stocks beat the market. A screen passes 75% of those, and 25% of the rest. A stock passes. What is the chance it beats the market?

options.why: You gave the hit rate: the chance of passing given a winner.
You divided the true passes by every stock, not by every pass.
You gave the base rate and ignored the screen.

feedback.correct: Of 100 stocks, 15 true passes and 20 false: $\tfrac{15}{35}$.
feedback.generic: Picture 100 stocks. How many pass, and how many of those are winners?

explain.text: In 100 stocks, 20 are winners and 15 pass; 80 are not and 20 pass. So $\tfrac{15}{35} = \tfrac37$. Bayes' rule gives $\tfrac{0.15}{0.15 + 0.2}$, the same.

items.title: The highest face is 3
items.question: Three fair dice are rolled. What is the chance that the highest face is 3?

options.why: You found the chance that all are at most 3. Take away all at most 2.
You made every die show 3.
You treated the six values of the highest face as equally likely.

feedback.correct: All at most 3, less all at most 2: $\tfrac{27 - 8}{216}$.
feedback.generic: Find the chance that all are at most 3, then take away all at most 2.

explain.text: All at most 3 has 27 outcomes; all at most 2 has 8. So the highest is exactly 3 in 19: $\tfrac{19}{216}$. Listing the 216 outcomes finds the same 19.

items.title: A 3, given 6
items.question: Two fair dice are rolled and the total is 6. What is the chance that at least one die shows 3?

options.why: You did not condition. That is the chance of the total and a 3 together.
You ignored the total. That is the chance of a 3 on any roll.
You listed unordered pairs as equally likely. Ordered pairs are.

feedback.correct: 1 of the 5 ordered pairs that make 6 show a 3.
feedback.generic: List the ordered pairs that make 6. Count those with a 3.

explain.text: The total 6 comes from (1, 5), (2, 4), (3, 3), (4, 2), (5, 1). One of those 5 shows a 3, so $\tfrac{1}{5}$.

items.title: First 5 or 6 wins
items.question: You and a friend take turns to roll a die, you first. The first to roll a 5 or a 6 wins. What is your chance of winning?

options.why: You ignored going first. The first roller has the edge.
You found your friend's chance.
You counted only your first roll.

feedback.generic: Win now, or both miss and the game starts again.

explain.text: Let $p$ be your chance: $p = \tfrac13 + \tfrac49 p$, so $p = \tfrac35$. The series $\tfrac13 \sum (\tfrac49)^k$ gives the same.

items.title: HHT or THH
items.question: A fair coin is tossed until HHT or THH appears. What is the chance that HHT comes first?

options.why: You needed the first three tosses to be HHT.
You treated the two patterns as equal. A T before the first HH sets up THH.
You found the chance that THH comes first.

feedback.correct: HHT wins only if the first two tosses are HH.
feedback.generic: What happens if a T comes before the first HH?

explain.text: If any T comes before the first HH, that HH completes THH first. So HHT wins only on HH at the start, with chance $\tfrac14$. An exact solve over the coin's states gives $\tfrac14$ too.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: At least one six in 2 rolls of a die
One card from a deck is an ace, king or queen

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.333, 0.306, 0.231.
feedback.generic: Work out each chance roughly; a complement is often quickest.

explain.text: A die shows 5 or 6: 0.333. At least one six in 2 rolls of a die: 0.306. One card from a deck is an ace, king or queen: 0.231.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: At least one ace in 3 cards drawn with replacement

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.375, 0.213, 0.167.
feedback.generic: Turn each event into a fraction, then compare.

explain.text: Exactly 1 head in 3 tosses: 0.375. At least one ace in 3 cards drawn with replacement: 0.213. Two dice show a double: 0.167.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: At least one ace in 6 cards drawn with replacement
A total of 5, 6 or 7 on two dice
One card from a deck is red or an ace

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.538, 0.417, 0.381.
feedback.generic: Use complements for the at-least-one events, and do not add chances.

explain.text: One card from a deck is red or an ace: 0.538. A total of 5, 6 or 7 on two dice: 0.417. At least one ace in 6 cards drawn with replacement: 0.381.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: A total of 11 or 12 on two dice

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.188, 0.083, 0.055.
feedback.generic: Count the ways for each, then divide by the outcomes.

explain.text: At least 4 heads in 5 tosses: 0.188. A total of 11 or 12 on two dice: 0.083. At least 8 heads in 10 tosses: 0.055.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: Two of 30 people share a birthday
At least one six in 8 rolls of a die
At least one ace in 10 cards dealt from a deck

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.767, 0.706, 0.587.
feedback.generic: Estimate each with a complement: one minus the chance of none.

explain.text: At least one six in 8 rolls of a die: 0.767. Two of 30 people share a birthday: 0.706. At least one ace in 10 cards dealt from a deck: 0.587.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.750, 0.688, 0.656.
feedback.generic: Do not assume the events tie because the expected counts match.

explain.text: At least 1 head in 2 tosses: 0.750. At least 2 heads in 4 tosses: 0.688. At least 3 heads in 6 tosses: 0.656.

items.title: A square root
items.question: Choose the tightest interval that holds $\sqrt{500}$.

options.why: This holds the value, but 22 to 23 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.
This sits wholly below the value, 22.36.
This sits wholly above the value, 22.36.

feedback.correct: 22 to 23 holds the value, 22.36, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Bracket the value from both sides first, then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: $22^2 = 484$ and $23^2 = 529$, so $\sqrt{500}$ lies between 22 and 23. In fact $\sqrt{500} = 10\sqrt5 \approx 22.36$. The interval 20 to 25 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less on the day.

items.title: Compound growth
items.question: Choose the tightest interval that holds $1.07^{12}$.

options.why: This sits wholly below the value, 2.252.
This holds the value, but 2.2 to 2.3 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.
This sits wholly above the value, 2.252.

feedback.correct: 2.2 to 2.3 holds the value, 2.252, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Bracket the value from both sides first, then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: $1.07^{10} \approx 1.97$, just under a doubling by the rule of 72. Two more years multiply by $1.07^2 \approx 1.145$, giving about 2.25. The interval 2 to 3 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less.

items.title: A rare event that never comes
items.question: An event has a 1% chance each day. Choose the tightest interval that holds the chance it never happens in 100 days, $0.99^{100}$.

options.why: This holds the value, but 0.35 to 0.38 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.
This sits wholly below the value, 0.366.
This sits wholly above the value, 0.366.

feedback.correct: 0.35 to 0.38 holds the value, 0.366, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Bracket the value from both sides first, then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: $(1 - \tfrac1n)^n$ is just under $\tfrac1e \approx 0.368$. The exact value is 0.366. The interval 0.2 to 0.5 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less.

items.title: Exactly half heads
items.question: A coin is tossed 20 times. Choose the tightest interval that holds the chance of exactly 10 heads, $\binom{20}{10} / 2^{20}$.

options.why: This holds the value, but 0.17 to 0.19 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.
This sits wholly below the value, 0.1762.
This sits wholly above the value, 0.1762.

feedback.correct: 0.17 to 0.19 holds the value, 0.1762, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Bracket the value from both sides first, then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: For $n$ tosses, exactly half heads is about $\sqrt{2 / (\pi n)}$, which is 0.178 for 20. The exact value is $184756 / 1048576 \approx 0.176$. The interval 0.1 to 0.3 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less.
